strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: supervised labeling (derived for free from generation prompts) enforces one-to-one concept–latent mappings, directly addressing feature splitting that plagues unsupervised SAE-based unlearning (SAeUron). This is a genuine, novel angle within SAE-based unlearning.

Empirical results are strong and multi-faceted: state-of-the-art on UnlearnCanvas (91.51% vs. 82.29% for SAeUron), improved sequential 9-object unlearning (92.4% vs. 64%), better multiplier robustness (Fig. 3), improved adversarial resilience under UnlearnDiffAtk, and competitive I2P nudity suppression.

The central claim—feature centralization—is validated quantitatively, not just asserted: k-NN classification (Fig. 5) shows a single top-scoring latent matches all-feature accuracy, and score-distribution analysis (Figs. 4, 10-12) shows a clear dominant peak versus the dispersed SAeUron baseline.

Extensive appendix ablations (10 model variants, global-CE alternative, post-TopK loss, decorrelation, hyperparameter sensitivity including the β=10 failure case) increase confidence in design choices and support reproducibility. Standard deviations across 4 seeds are reported, and the 9.22% gain far exceeds the ±0.4 seed variance.

The authors discovered and corrected an inconsistency in the SAeUron metric computation and recomputed baselines, and they are honest about failure modes (e.g., the base single-latent setup performing worse than SAeUron on nudity before the TOP2 variant, and struggles with style-blended objects like flames and jellyfish).
weaknesses: Scope of the supervision is a fundamental trade-off that is not discussed as a limitation: SAEMNESIA can only unlearn concepts present in its predefined concept dictionary Φ; unlearning a new concept requires (re)training the SAE. This materially weakens the practical story relative to unsupervised methods and deserves explicit treatment, not just a passing note that labels are 'free'.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: experiments are confined to SD v1.5 / SD v1.4 on the synthetic UnlearnCanvas benchmark (whose prompts already provide the label structure the method relies on) plus one I2P experiment. Generalization to real, unconstrained prompts, other architectures, or concepts outside the training dictionary is untested.

Label quality is assumed rather than analyzed: every spatial patch of an image generated with 'An image of {object} in {style}' is labeled with the object/style, even patches that plausibly depict background or style only. The paper does not quantify how noisy such prompt-derived labels are or how label noise affects the learned mappings.

Some headline numbers are soft: the '96.7% hyperparameter search reduction' follows almost by construction from restricting to a single latent (210 vs. 7 evaluations), and the adversarial result still degrades substantially (73.3%→28.3%), even if less than the baseline; framing should reflect this.

Key deployment details are deferred or thin: FID comparisons appear only in appendix tables, the best variant is selected via hyperparameter search (a search cost partially offsetting the claimed efficiency gain), and there is no explicit statement about code release, which limits reproducibility of the full pipeline (activation extraction, fine-tuning schedule, multipliers).

Presentation has rough edges: duplicated sentences on page 6 ('The performance gains stem from...'), metric naming inconsistency between 'monosemanticity' claims and the one-latent-per-concept framing (which is closer to feature centralization than monosemanticity), and many similarly named variants (OO/OS/DC/CA/FS/FT) that make the main results hard to track.

strengths: The core idea is clearly motivated: supervised labeling of activations during SAE training to enforce one-to-one concept-latent mappings, directly addressing feature splitting in unsupervised SAEs (e.g., SAeUron). The supervision is cheap since labels are derived from generation prompts.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: UnlearnCanvas benchmark with UA/IRA/CRA metrics, uniform multiplier sweeps, k-NN validation of feature centralization, sequential unlearning over 9 objects, adversarial robustness under UnlearnDiffAtk, and I2P nudity evaluation.

The computational-efficiency argument is concrete and verifiable: reducing a 210-evaluation (7 multipliers x 30 latent combinations) search to 7 evaluations is a genuine, well-explained benefit of single-latent steering.

Appendix contains a substantial amount of supporting material: seed standard deviations, ablations over 10 model variants, score-distribution histograms for multiple concepts, Cats-Dogs interference analysis, and full nudity-detection tables.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is incremental. The 'supervised SAE' amounts to adding a sigmoid cross-entropy-style loss on assigned latents plus a Pearson-correlation decorrelation penalty on top of a standard TopK SAE. The main novelty relative to SAeUron is the supervised labels, which the paper itself notes 'come at no additional cost'; there is little architectural or algorithmic depth beyond this.

A fundamental limitation is insufficiently confronted: the method requires the concept set to be known a priori (concepts, and even concept groups for the decorrelation loss, must be defined before training), and the hidden layer cardinality bounds representable concepts. Real-world unlearning requests typically arrive post-hoc and are open-ended. The paper never evaluates erasure of concepts outside the training concept set, and this constraint is not honestly discussed as a limitation.

The abstract and conclusion oversell results relative to the appendix. The abstract claims the method 'effectively removes nudity when evaluated with I2P,' but Appendix 6.11 and Table 9 show the base SAEMNESIA performs poorly (47 detections vs. SAeUron's 18); the reported 9 detections require a special TOP2 variant that steers two latents, which directly contradicts the paper's central single-latent thesis and is only discovered in the appendix.

The adversarial robustness framing is generous: SAEMNESIA still drops from 73.30% to 28.30% unlearning accuracy under attack. It is better than the baseline's collapse (26.19% to 2.22%), but describing a ~45-point drop as establishing resilience overstates the finding.

The '96.7% hyperparameter search reduction' claim is narrower than presented: it counts only the inference-time multiplier/latent search, while the training pipeline itself involved selecting among at least 10 variants (Table 4), choosing between fine-tuning vs. from-scratch, and tuning loss coefficients; moreover, training is brittle (beta = 10 produces completely white images per Appendix 6.10), so substantial tuning burden is arguably shifted rather than eliminated.

The best-reported configuration (OS-DC-CA-FT) is a fine-tuned model with searched hyperparameters; the from-scratch variant performs worse (90.85 vs 91.51), and some variants underperform the baseline (e.g., OO-GCE at 79.9, OS-TK-CA-FT at 66.85 UA in Table 5), suggesting the headline numbers depend on careful variant selection.

Presentation quality is uneven: duplicated sentences ('The performance gains stem from the stronger concept-latent associations...' appears twice on page 6), typos ('similiar', 'consist'), and notation collisions (gamma is used both for the DC weight in Eq. (7)/(9) and for unlearning multipliers in Eq. (10)), plus an unexplained discrepancy where the appendix says the DC weight 'gamma = 0.1' while Eq. (9) defines the loss as L_DC.

Sequential unlearning is tested on only 9 objects hand-picked by the authors, and the metric computation for the closest baseline had to be recomputed by the authors themselves due to an 'inconsistency' in the public SAeUron implementation; while this is disclosed, it weakens direct comparability of the headline 9.22% improvement.
The claims that the method is 'architecture agnostic' and transfers to other T2I models are asserted but not demonstrated: all main experiments use SD v1.5 (with SD v1.4 only for the I2P experiment).

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: feature splitting in unsupervised SAEs makes diffusion model concept unlearning expensive and imprecise. The proposed supervised SAE (SAEMNESIA) with a Concept Assignment loss, decorrelation constraint, and L1 sparsity is a clean and well-motivated solution that directly enforces one-to-one concept-latent mappings.

The empirical case is strong and multi-faceted: state-of-the-art results on UnlearnCanvas (91.51% avg vs. SAeUron's 82.29%), superior sequential unlearning of 9 objects (92.4% vs 64%), improved robustness to UnlearnDiffAtk adversarial prefixes, and competitive nudity suppression on I2P. This breadth of evaluation goes beyond a single benchmark.

The central claim — feature centralization — is validated quantitatively, not just asserted: score-distribution analyses (Figs. 4, 10-12) show dominant peaks, k-NN experiments (Fig. 5) confirm the top-1 latent carries nearly all concept information, and reduced sensitivity to the multiplier magnitude (Fig. 3, smaller multipliers in Tab. 3) supports the mechanism.
The claimed 96.67% reduction in hyperparameter search (7 vs. 210 evaluations) is a concrete, verifiable practical benefit of the interpretable representation.

The appendix is unusually thorough: seed-wise standard deviations, ten ablation variants (Tab. 4-6), Cats-vs-Dogs concept interference analysis, per-object multiplier tables, and per-category nudity results. Notably, the authors honestly report failure cases (e.g., weak single-latent nudity performance, requiring a TOP2 variant; struggles with styles that blend into objects), which strengthens credibility.
The paper transparently discloses that baseline SAeUron metrics were recomputed due to an inconsistency in its public implementation, rather than silently comparing against published numbers.
weaknesses: The supervision requirement is a significant scope limitation. SAEMNESIA requires labeled activations for every concept to be unlearned, generated from structured prompts (80 per object-style pair). This means new unlearning requests necessitate SAE training data collection and retraining/fine-tuning, which partially undercuts the 'efficiency' narrative and limits applicability to open-ended, user-specified concepts. The paper does not evaluate how the SAE behaves on concepts absent from training.

The method is an inference-time intervention and does not modify model weights; the 'forgotten' capability remains recoverable (e.g., by disabling the SAE). This is arguably weaker than true unlearning for safety-critical deployment, and the paper could discuss this more explicitly, particularly given safety-framed claims about adversarial robustness — UA still drops substantially under attack (73.30% to 28.30%).

Evaluation is confined to SD v1.4/v1.5 and the UnlearnCanvas ecosystem. The 'architecture agnostic' claim (Sec. 3) is asserted but not demonstrated on other T2I models or newer model families, leaving generalizability unverified.

Since all SAEMNESIA results are produced under a self-corrected metric computation, cross-paper comparability of Tab. 1 (ESD, UCE, SPM, etc., presumably using published numbers) is imperfect; ideally all baselines would be recomputed under the corrected protocol.

The feature centralization proxy (CA loss + L1) and the score-based latent assignment (Eqs. 4-5) are heuristic; there is no theoretical or controlled analysis of when one-to-one mappings fail (e.g., the TOP2 nudity case suggests the mapping is fragile under imbalanced data). The threshold condition z > µ in Eq. (10) is ad hoc.

No explicit statement about releasing code or training data pipelines, which matters for reproducibility given the specialized supervised training procedure; also, FID values (e.g., 110-124) are high across methods, and image quality impact under intervention deserves more discussion.

Minor presentation issues: duplicated sentences in Sec. 4.2, and the 'concepts = features' terminology conflation is acknowledged but occasionally obscures the contribution relative to prior monosemanticity work.

strengths: The core idea is clear and well-motivated: supervised concept-latent labeling during SAE training to enforce one-to-one mappings, directly targeting the feature-splitting problem that makes unsupervised SAE-based unlearning (SAeUron) computationally expensive and prone to side effects.

Comprehensive evaluation: UnlearnCanvas (objects and styles), sequential unlearning for 9 objects, adversarial robustness under both white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) attacks, I2P nudity suppression, held-out concept generalization, concept interference analysis (Dogs vs. Cats), inference-cost analysis, and a preliminary second backbone (SDXL-Turbo).

The efficiency claim is concrete and verifiable: reducing the multiplier/latent-combination search from 210 to 7 evaluations (96.67% reduction) follows directly from the one-latent-per-concept design, and inference overhead is actually slightly lower than the baseline (1.89% vs 2.56%).

Good mechanistic validation of the central claim: score-distribution histograms (Fig. 4, Fig. 9), k-NN classification showing a single latent matches all-feature accuracy (Fig. 5), and attention-map visualizations across timesteps (Fig. 7) support that feature centralization actually occurs.

Honest and substantive limitations section covering closed-vocabulary constraints, within-group interference, scalability to 20K+ concepts, and architecture generality; the extensive ablations over ~10 SAE variants (Tables 7-11) improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The contribution is a fairly incremental extension of a single recent baseline (SAeUron); the novelty is the supervised labeling of concepts during SAE training, and the conceptual distance from the prior work is modest. Comparisons to non-SAE baselines rely on previously reported numbers rather than controlled re-runs.

Key limitations of the supervision assumption surface in the results: on held-out (unseen) styles, UA is only 53.07% vs. SAeUron's 50.69% (Table 17), indicating the method largely does not generalize beyond its supervised concept set; and on nudity, the single-latent variant underperforms SAeUron (47 vs. 18 detections), requiring a TOP2 variant with an extreme multiplier (-600), which partially undercuts the headline one-latent-per-concept story.

The SDXL-Turbo transfer results (Table 12) are weak: SAEmnesia improves UA over the unsupervised SAE but IRA drops to 45.15%, and the authors themselves note the evaluation protocol is noisy on that backbone, so architectural generality remains essentially unverified.

Sequential object unlearning is evaluated on a setting constructed by the authors (UnlearnCanvas only defines sequential style unlearning), so the 28.4% scalability claim lacks an established benchmark; the fixed choices (m=7 multipliers, l=30 latent combinations, gamma=-1, final 25 denoising steps) are not thoroughly justified.

Statistical treatment is asymmetric: standard deviations over 4 seeds are reported only for SAEmnesia (Table 5), not for SAeUron, making the +9.22 average improvement harder to interpret; UA std of ±2.6 suggests some gaps may be within noise for individual metrics.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'more effective NSFW-content suppression' in the contributions while the flagship single-latent configuration is worse than the baseline (Table 13), and the overall-average comparison (94.85%) is only achieved because style unlearning is near-ceiling for both methods.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental coverage: the paper evaluates on UnlearnCanvas (objects and styles), sequential unlearning, both white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) adversarial attacks, I2P nudity suppression, held-out concept generalization, and a preliminary SDXL-Turbo transfer, with an extensive appendix including standard deviations over 4 seeds and ablations over 10 method variants.

The core idea is sensible and directly validated: supervised concept-latent assignment demonstrably concentrates concept information into single latents, supported by the k-NN experiment (Figure 5), score-distribution histograms (Figure 4, Figure 9), and the much smaller required steering multipliers (average -6.6 vs. -21.25 for SAeUron).
Honest limitations section that correctly identifies the closed-vocabulary constraint, within-group interference, and scalability concerns, plus a thoughtful impact statement.

Consistent and meaningful gains over the SAE-based baseline SAeUron on object unlearning (+9.22 avg) and large improvements in sequential 9-object unlearning (92.4% vs. 64%), with code/checkpoint comparability (using SAeUron's public checkpoints).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the contribution is largely an incremental extension of SAeUron — the concept–latent score function (Eq. 4), the TopK SAE setup, the activation extraction pipeline, and the evaluation protocol are all taken from Cywiński & Deja (2025), with the new element being supervised BCE plus decorrelation losses added on top. The 'supervised SAE' idea itself is not conceptually new.

The closed-vocabulary supervision fundamentally weakens the claimed significance: concepts must be labeled during SAE training with synthetic anchor prompts, limiting applicability to benchmark-style concept sets (20 objects + 50 styles). The held-out generalization result (Table 17, UA ~53%) shows erasure of unseen concepts is substantially weaker, and the claimed '96.67% hyperparameter reduction' is an artificial accounting (210 vs. 7 grid evaluations) that ignores the 27-configuration hyperparameter sweep used for training the SAE itself.

Evidence of fragility in the one-latent-per-concept story: single-latent nudity unlearning actually underperforms SAeUron (47 vs. 18 detections), and the rescue (SAEmnesia-TOP2) requires an extreme multiplier of -600, contradicting the narrative of stable, single-latent control. The headline model (OS-DC-CA-FT) shows 10 Cats-Dogs overlap timesteps — no better than the baseline (Table 11) — so the known concept-interference problem is not actually mitigated in the reported configuration.

Cherry-picking concerns: SAEmnesia is the best of 10 explored variants; several alternatives (e.g., OO-GCE-FT at 79.9 avg.) underperform the SAeUron baseline. On object unlearning alone, SalUn (94.28) still beats SAEmnesia (91.51), so the SOTA claim relies on averaging in the easier style-unlearning setting.

Weak transfer evidence beyond SD v1.5/v1.4: the SDXL-Turbo results (Table 12) show IRA collapsing to 45.15 (far worse than doing nothing) and an average of 54.39 vs. the trivial 50.0 baseline — i.e., barely above chance with severe collateral damage. The adversarial robustness gain is real but modest (40-point drop under white-box attack persists). Training cost also increases ~5.4× over the unsupervised SAE (Table 3).

Reliance on classifier-based UA/IRA/CRA metrics and synthetic prompt structures raises questions about how well 'unlearning' generalizes to natural user prompts; qualitative figures show failures on concepts blended with styles (flames, jellyfish), acknowledged only in the appendix.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a concrete weakness of unsupervised SAE-based unlearning (feature splitting / weak concept-latent mappings in SAeUron) and proposes a targeted remedy via supervised concept assignment, decorrelation, and sparsity losses.

Comprehensive and multi-dimensional evaluation: UnlearnCanvas object and style unlearning (Tables 1, 14, 15), sequential unlearning for both objects and styles, adversarial robustness under both white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) attacks, I2P nudity suppression, and held-out concept generalization (Table 17).

Good mechanistic validation of the central claim: feature importance score distributions (Fig. 4, 9), k-NN classification showing a single latent nearly matches all latents (Fig. 5), and patch-level activation visualizations (Fig. 7) collectively support that supervised training centralizes concept information.

Extensive ablations over 10 method variants (Tables 7-9, A.8-A.9), hyperparameter details, multi-seed standard deviations (A.4), computational cost breakdowns (A.3), and honest reporting of failure cases (e.g., flames/jellyfish, Dogs-vs-Cats entanglement, weak single-latent nudity result requiring TOP2).
Transparent limitations section covering the closed-vocabulary constraint, within-group interference, concept-count scalability, and restricted backbone coverage, plus a responsible impact statement.
weaknesses: The 'single-latent erasure' narrative is somewhat overstated: the headline results use per-object searched multipliers (Table 6), and the nudity setting requires steering two latents with an extreme multiplier (-600), which weakens the strict one-to-one story that motivates the 96.67% hyperparameter-reduction claim (itself a simple arithmetic framing of 7 vs. 210 evaluations).

Evaluation relies heavily on ViT-classifier-based metrics (UA/IRA/CRA); classifier-based unlearning accuracy can conflate image changes with actual concept removal. FID and qualitative results partially mitigate this, but no human evaluation or semantic-verification study is provided.

Direct experimental comparisons are essentially limited to SAeUron (using its public checkpoints); other methods are quoted from prior benchmark numbers without controlled re-evaluation, and SalUn actually beats SAEmnesia on object-unlearning average (94.28 vs 91.51), so the 'state-of-the-art' framing depends on combining object and style tasks.

Methodological novelty is moderate: adding supervised losses to SAE training echoes supervised approaches such as Concept Steerers; the contribution is primarily an empirical/understanding advance (feature centralization) rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Training cost is substantially higher than the baseline (~385 ms vs ~71 ms per step, ~5.4x, Table 3), which is reported but not emphasized relative to the claimed efficiency gains; and the training-time hyperparameter grid search (27 configurations) somewhat undercuts the efficiency framing.

Supervision depends on anchor prompts with a narrow template distribution, and held-out generalization gains are modest (73.75 vs 72.32 avg on unseen styles), leaving open questions about robustness of the concept-latent binding beyond the curated concept vocabulary.
